title: Lectio divina
hookLine: an old monastic way: read a short passage, notice a word, ponder it, rest

cards: How do you read now? Probably fast: scrolling, skimming, headlines, the first two lines of a message and then the next one.
In a medieval monastery, a monk sits with a book and reads a single sentence aloud, quietly, to himself. Then again. And again.

He isn't trying to finish, or to learn a fact for a test. He's trying to taste it. The monks had a word for this, taken from the way a cow chews the same mouthful over and over, slowly, all afternoon: rumination.
And they had a name for the whole practice. It means sacred reading.

teach.b: Lectio divina is Latin: divine reading, sacred reading. Saint Benedict, who wrote a rule for monks in the sixth century, set aside hours every day for it.
In the twelfth century a monk named Guigo, the head of a Carthusian monastery in the French Alps, described it as a ladder with four rungs.

First, lectio, reading: you read a short passage slowly, often aloud, and notice which word or phrase catches you. Second, meditatio, pondering: you turn that word over, chew it, ask what it's saying to you today.
Third, oratio, prayer: you answer God, in your own words, about what you've noticed. Fourth, contemplatio, contemplation, the hardest to explain, because it isn't really doing anything. You rest.
You stop talking and simply stay, the way you'd sit with someone you love without needing to speak.

Guigo put it in a picture: reading puts the food in your mouth, pondering chews it, prayer tastes it, and contemplation is the sweetness itself. The point isn't to cover much. A whole morning might be spent on one line.
That's hard when you want to get through it, but lectio divina says the opposite: go slowly enough and one word is enough. For centuries it lived mostly in monasteries.
Today Catholics, Anglicans and many Protestants use it, alone or in small groups, where people read a passage aloud three or four times and each shares the one word that stayed with them.
It works best with a short passage; a single verse from the Psalms is plenty. Try this one: "Be still, and know that I am God."

how: Monks and nuns practice lectio divina daily, and many Catholic, Anglican and Protestant Christians use it alone or in small groups, reading a short passage slowly several times, sharing a word that stood out, praying, and resting in silence.

games.q: you're reading a psalm the old monastic way. one word has caught you. what do you do next?
o: move on to the next verse.
stay with that word and turn it over.
look it up in a dictionary.
games.why: you stay: meditatio, pondering, chewing it over. then you pray about it, and then you rest.

practice: Say that verse, be still, and know that I am God, four times: first slowly, noticing which word catches you, maybe still, maybe know; second, turning that one word over.
Third, if you pray, answer God about it; if you don't, answer yourself. Fourth, say it one last time, then rest in the quiet without doing anything at all.

wordCard.voice: Lectio divina. Latin for sacred reading: read, ponder, pray, rest, with a very few words.

orig.note: Latin: divine or sacred reading. Benedict's Rule already uses the phrase.

carryVoice: Your line: one word is enough. Tomorrow, a nightly look back at the day. Day one hundred and one, done.
